BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: A closed upper low continues to impact the area Thursday through Friday. Continuous valley rain and mountain snow is expected, beginning to taper off Friday. 0.20 inches of rain will fall by early Friday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Valley rain and mountain snow tonight, ending overnight in eastern OR but showers continuing in ID Tuesday morning.
- 12-18 hours drying then another Pacific storm Wednesday through Thursday, colder and windier, but not as wet as current storm. Boise may see snowflakes but no snow accumulation Thursday morning.
- Another Pacific storm with rain and snow Saturday through Sunday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Two main storms through Thursday: the current wetter and warmer one through tonight, ending in OR before sunrise and in ID Tuesday afternoon, and another colder, windier, but less-wet storm Wednesday through Thursday. Pcpn with the current storm has been moving only slowly eastward near the OR/ID border today but will move faster tonight as it gets into ID. Snow level will be 5500-6500 feet during heaviest pcpn, then lower to 5000 feet as pcpn ends. Total QPF should be .50 to .80 inch in northern mountains and .25 to .50 inch in the valleys and southern mountains, except less than .25 inch in Harney County. Wet snow may accumulate 1-3 inches at pass levels in northern areas, with McCall receiving 1-2 inches. After 12-18 hours of drying, rain and snow from the next Pacific storm will reach eastern OR pre- dawn Wednesday, and western ID later Wednesday, continuing in all areas Wednesday night, then decreasing to showers, mainly of snow, on Thursday. Snow level with that storm will be 3000-4000 feet, but total pcpn will only be .10 to .30 inch in northern mountains and in the Camas Prairie, with .05 to .15 inch in the valleys. Snowfall should be 1-4 inches in the mountains and an inch or less in the valleys. Boise may see its first snowflakes Thursday morning but no accumulation is expected. This second storm will also bring stronger wind, from the southeast 15 to 25 mph with gusts to 30 mph on Wednesday, decreasing to 10-15 mph from the west or northwest Thursday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A closed upper low continues to impact the area Thursday through Friday. Continuous valley rain and mountain snow is expected, beginning to taper off Friday. 0.20 inches of rain will fall by early Friday. Latest long-range guidance has snow levels hanging in the 3500-4500 ft range through Saturday. Valleys may see a rain/snow mix Friday morning, before precipitation completely tapers off by late Friday/early Saturday. Most central ID mountains are forecast to receiver around 1-2 inches of snow, up to 3-7 inches in the S- Central ID mountains, and around 3-7 inches again in Eastern OR mountains. By early Saturday, the system will steer out of our area and a ridge develops overhead. This brief dry period will be limited, as long-term guidance has another Pacific upper trough moving into the northwest and into the eastern OR side by late Saturday. Slight chances of valley rain or rain/snow mix and mountain snow showers are forecast for late Saturday through early Monday, with higher terrain areas seeing the bulk of total precip and snow.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: On Thursday, we expect some weak ridging with near-average temperatures. The next system looks to move in starting Friday, but should progress slower than the early week system.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Increasing confidence in gusty winds across the Front Range mountains and foothills late Tuesday night into Wednesday. Some more isolated stronger wind gusts could reach the lower elevations on Wednesday.
- Remaining mild and dry across the plains over the next several days.
- Chances for mountain snow late Tuesday night into Wednesday morning, and again Friday into Saturday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: GOES-19 satellite imagery shows mostly clear skies this afternoon after dense fog this morning across northeast Colorado. Today and Tuesday will be dry for the area and mild with ridging aloft. High temperatures on the plains are forecast to be in the low to mid 60s. High-resolution guidance is in good agreement that a Denver Cyclone is likely to form on Tuesday. As a result, some locations on the eastern plains could see wind gusts of 25-35 mph tomorrow afternoon. As the week progresses, high temperatures on the plains will cool down into the 50s. By late Tuesday evening into early Wednesday morning, troughing should move into the state. This will open the door for snow chances in the high country. Most locations will only see a dusting at most with limited moisture in place, but the Park Range and northern Gore Range could get up to 2 inches of snow given favorable upslope.

By early Wednesday morning as any precipitation begins to wind down, the ingredients for a Bora event could come together for our area. Cold air advection, little wind shear, and strong near-westerly cross barrier flow is expected to develop with mixed layer winds reaching or even exceeding 50-60 kts through much of Wednesday morning and into the early afternoon. On Wednesday morning, models show northeast CO near the right exit region of a jet aloft as well as strong subsidence which would aid in increasing wind speeds. Model soundings from the latest RRFS runs have shown a stable layer around 650-700 mb, so this could be something to watch for in terms of any enhancement of winds. Some potential limiting factors include only a very weak surface pressure gradient and the jet positioning. By Wednesday afternoon, the jet could be overhead, which would likely confine the strong wind gusts to far northern portions of our area and into Wyoming.

REFS and NBM mean max wind gusts on Wednesday now show peak wind gusts of at least 60-65 mph for the northern Front Range mountains and 50-60 mph for the northern Front Range foothills. The high resolution guidance that has come in today is hinting at the potential for a few stronger wind gusts to make it down into the typical windy areas in these setups along the Front Range such as the Hwy 93 corridor as well as northern Weld County. This solution is still rather uncertain, but as of now we expect wind gusts to stay below high wind criteria for the Hwy 93 corridor.

As is typical in these setups, there could be some narrow channels of 30-40 mph wind gusts for the Denver metro if the ingredients can come together. In general, confidence is increasing in the potential for a high wind event for portions of the high country north of I-70 including the higher terrain of Larimer and Boulder counties on Wednesday morning and potentially lasting into the afternoon. Therefore, we have issued a High Wind Watch for the northern Front Range foothills from 2am to 2pm Wednesday. The High Wind Watch could need to be expanded in future packages if confidence increases in the peak wind gusts meeting criteria at the highest elevations.

On Thursday, we expect some weak ridging with near-average temperatures. The next system looks to move in starting Friday, but should progress slower than the early week system. Once again, this system will favor the high country for any precipitation with southwest to west flow aloft. Precipitation chances will likely continue on Saturday. Ensemble guidance shows that the plains has a very low chance for some light scattered rain from this system. At this time, snow chances remain near zero for Denver through at least this weekend. Therefore, we are nearly guaranteed to have a top 5 latest first snow for Denver. With another strong jet aloft moving through and a tightening pressure gradient, we could be in for another period of stronger wind gusts Friday afternoon into Saturday. From Sunday onward, a more zonal pattern looks to be in place with signs in ensemble guidance of near-average to below average temperatures becoming more likely.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Monday...A split trough aloft moves across the Rockies, with most energy and 500-300 mb and 700-500 mb quasigeostrophic forcing either north of our counties over Montana or south of our counties over New Mexico, though scattered showers of rain and/or snow will likely fall in minimal amounts over our counties.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Patchy fog will again be possible into Tuesday morning, mainly for locations in the Nebraska Panhandle.

- A High Wind Watch is now in effect for the Wind Prone areas of southeast Wyoming and some of the adjacent sub-wind prone areas along highway 287 and Interstate 25 north of Wheatland. Gusts over 65+ MPH are possible late Tuesday night through Wednesday evening.
- A chance for a few rain and snow showers Tuesday night into Wednesday, mainly across portions of Carbon and Albany Counties. Another chance for rain and snow possible late Friday into Saturday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Low clouds and fog plagued portions of the Nebraska Panhandle earlier this morning, especially along the North Platte River Valley where visibilities below 1/4 of a mile were observed. This has since dissipated based off visible satellite, which has lead to rapid warming of surface temperatures with many locations soaring into the low to mid 60s into this afternoon across the Nebraska Panhandle and locations along and east of I-25 in SE Wyoming. The anomalous warmth and dry weather is due to the presence of a broad upper-level ridge centered over the Central United States characterized by 500 mb heights exceeding the 95th percentile relative to climatology. Expect overall dry and tranquil weather this afternoon and into the evening hours under weak southerly surface flow as lee troughing begins to occur over the High Plains gradually shifting winds to more out of the SE overnight into Tuesday morning. The weak SE upslope flow is expected to result in another round of fog (potentially dense) across the southern half of the Nebraska Panhandle as winds remain rather light and low-level moisture characterized by dewpoints in the 40s present. There has been a strong signal amongst high-resolution model guidance that the greatest coverage of dense fog will be situated along the North Platte River Valley, similar to the past few nights. To reflect these trends, have extended areas of fog after 06Z as far west as Torrington where lies the highest confidence. Overall, low temperatures overnight will remain quite mild for mid-November, with lows mostly staying above freezing in the 30s (we are typically down well into the 20s this time of year).

The upper-level ridge axis continues to shift east of our area tomorrow, giving us one last unseasonably mild and mostly dry day before we transition into a cooler, windier, and more active pattern Tuesday night and into the end of the work week. Under mostly to partly sunny skies, highs again will reach the upper 50s to low 60s east of the I-25 corridor, with slightly cooler temperatures over our western counties which will see an earlier onset of greater cloud coverage as our next system ejects north and east out of the Great Basin.

Ahead of this weak open wave that brushes by our far western counties tomorrow evening into Wednesday morning, 700 mb gradient flow is expected to increase up to 65-75 knots by late Tuesday evening. Unsurprisingly, this will also bring us noticeably breezier conditions overnight Tuesday into Wednesday across SE Wyoming, with the strongest winds in the usual wind-prone areas of Arlington, Bordeaux, and the I-80 Summit. Model cross-sections continue to indicate a mountain-top stable layer (denoted by tightly packed isentropes at mountain top), along with a mountain wave signature in the omega field. Further, 700 mb Craig to Casper geopotential height differences are expected to increase from ~60 meters overnight Tuesday, to around 80 meters by early Wednesday morning, which is the most impressive high-wind signature we have seen so far this season. Our in-house high wind guidance has consistently shown > 60% probabilities of both Arlington and Bordeaux exceeding high wind criteria overnight Tuesday into Wednesday morning before the lifting shortwave trough and associated speed maximum exits our region. Will continue the High Wind Watch for the wind-prone regions of Carbon and Albany Counties, along with Platte County and the western portion of Laramie County starting overnight Tuesday through Wednesday evening to account for high winds, including the possibility for a few gusts exceeding 70 mph.

While the high wind takes the cake in terms of weather highlights in the short term period, portions of Carbon, Albany, and Converse Counties will likely see some light precipitation, falling in the form of snow within the Sierra Madre and Snowy Ranges, and rain transitioning to a rain/snow mix or very wet snow in areas above 7000 feet overnight Tuesday into Wednesday morning. Not expecting any snow accumulation at lower elevations (places such as Rawlins), however can expect 2-4 inches on some of the higher peaks (though below advisory criteria).

With winds generally weakening overnight Wednesday into early Thursday morning, combined with mostly clear skies behind the departing system, overnight lows will actually be seasonably chilly mainly in the mid to upper 20s across the area. Finally a true taste of the windy Wyoming winter weather that we have been waiting to see (just minus the snow for most).

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Thursday...The relatively balmy weather for the latter half of November, continues with strong southwest flow aloft inducing surface lee troughing. Gusty south and southwest winds will persist based on projected gradients. Still dry with the paucity of low and mid level moisture availability. 700 mb temperatures near 1 Celsius will yield maximum temperatures from the mid 40s to mid 50s.

Friday...An initial shortwave trough aloft, or atmospheric perturbation, will encroach on our western counties early in the day, spreading widespread orographic and dynamically driven rain and snow showers across Carbon County Wyoming and our Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges. Then, after midday, the scattered to numerous rain and snow showers will spread eastward across the rest of southeast Wyoming, with the typical downsloping limiting shower coverage along and east of the Laramie Range and Interstate 25 corridor. A typical blustery cool day is on tap, with maximum temperatures in the 40s to lower 50s.

Interestingly, climatologically, November 20th, 1900, is the latest first measurable snowfall event for Cheyenne in the Autumn, with 0.1 inches of snow or greater. The verdict is still out as to whether Cheyenne will officially see the 0.1 inch snowfall criteria met this day, due to uncertainties, as it is a coin flip whether or not a rogue snow shower affects Cheyenne. Unfortunately, downsloping and the speed and location of the shortwave trough aloft passage and its associated cold front, will limit any precipitation accumulation east of I-25, although our Snowy, Sierra Madre and Laramie Ranges will fare better with decent accumulations possibly in at least Winter Weather Advisory criteria and possibly more.

Saturday...As the shortwave trough aloft sweeps quickly into the Plains states, strong westerly flow aloft develops across our counties, with our typical wind prone locations such as Arlington, Bordeaux and the I-80 Summit possibly seeing strong winds, possibly exceeding High Wind criteria. Drying out from west to east during the day in the wake of the shortwave trough aloft. Cheyenne may indeed see its first measurable snow before noon on November 21st. Five days before Thanksgiving, an even colder day is anticipated with readings from the mid 30s to mid 40s with 700 mb temperatures around 6 Celsius.

Sunday...The progressive pattern synoptically continues, with our flow aloft once again backing to southwest in advance of the next approaching shortwave trough aloft over southern Nevada, backing our surface winds to southeasterly to the east of the Interstate 25 corridor. Paucity of low and mid level moisture spells dry conditions continuing. Not quite as cold with highs from the upper 30s to upper 40s, based on 700 mb temperature trends and less cloud cover compared to Saturday.

Monday...A split trough aloft moves across the Rockies, with most energy and 500-300 mb and 700-500 mb quasigeostrophic forcing either north of our counties over Montana or south of our counties over New Mexico, though scattered showers of rain and/or snow will likely fall in minimal amounts over our counties. Temperatures similar to Sunday.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Forecast models continue to show another system arriving late Thursday night through Saturday morning. Models still show an open wave setup.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - The next system will bring valley rain and mountain snow on Tuesday and Wednesday, followed by another storm system on Friday and Saturday.
- Wind gusts of 25-45 mph will be common Tuesday afternoon and evening.
- Mountain passes could see adverse travel conditions Tuesday night and Wednesday morning due to snow.
- Temperatures will trend downward late week, with colder air delivering the first freezing temperatures for some desert valleys.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: SHOWERS TUESDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY MORNING

Dry conditions with increasing clouds are expected today. The next system moves across the area Tuesday afternoon through Wednesday morning. Strong southwesterly winds develop Tuesday ahead of the system. Gusts tomorrow could reach 45 mph especially across the southwest half of the area. Showers and perhaps a few embedded thunderstorms develop Tuesday afternoon and continue through Wednesday morning. Rainfall amounts in the valleys are generally under 0.5" with most places seeing a trace-0.25". Snow levels will start around 9-10kft when showers arrive and drop to around 6-7kft overnight. The southern mountains and Utah mountains will be favored for this event. Snowfall amounts above 9kft will range from 4-10" with lesser amounts for lower elevations. The other mountain ranges could expect more like 1-4". Blowing snow and snow packed roads may cause travel impacts on the mountain passes Tuesday night.

Showers will taper off around daybreak Wednesday, as this system exits the region. A few lingering snow showers will continue along the Divide Wednesday morning. Cooler and drier conditions develop on Wednesday with temperatures 10 to 15 degrees colder behind the front. A weak transitory ridge moves overhead Wednesday and Thursday as another more organized system comes ashore out west.

Forecast models continue to show another system arriving late Thursday night through Saturday morning. Models still show an open wave setup. Precipitation totals continue to vary by model run, with the central and northern mountains of Colorado picking up additional snow in the latest runs. Differences among the models with regards to strength and timing keep confidence low attm. Most of the moisture is expected to arrive ahead of the cold front, making timing critical. Snow levels could drop to some valley floors Friday night into Saturday morning. For now, however, the specifics remain uncertain.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Beyond this weekend, another broad trough appears to be on deck for early next week, though it is still far too early for details to become clear.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Generally mild weather through Tuesday.
- Quick-moving system passes through Tues Night-Weds, bringing snow to the Continental Divide and gusty winds to all of SE Colorado.
- Another slightly stronger system to bring mountain snow and wind Thursday night through Friday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: An upper-level ridge will continue moving over our area today and tomorrow, giving us relatively mild and dry conditions through the next 24 hours.
Temperatures this afternoon will remain on the cool side, thanks to the fog and cloud cover from this morning. Expect highs across the area to generally remain in the 50s to around 60.

For Tuesday, fewer clouds and southerly winds into the region will allow for temperatures to climb considerably. Highs will be in the mid-high 60s over most of the eastern plains, while the valleys remain in the high-50s. Gusty southwest flow will set in across the area, stronger over the far SE plains, with showers starting to move into the southwest mountains by early evening ahead of our next incoming system.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Moving into mid-week, a quick-moving upper trough will pass through our region, starting Tuesday Night and lasting into early Wednesday. Showers will start over the San Juans, spreading to the rest of the higher terrain and parts of the San Luis Valley overnight. The system has trended faster over the last few sets of model runs, and a bit more north, meaning that impacts have generally decreased. As of now, latest snow totals show localized 3-6 inch accumulations over the San Juans, and lighter amounts (generally an inch or less) over the rest of the mountain peaks. The San Luis Valley should see mostly rain, and currently little to no snow accumulation is expected. Snow levels should remain above 7kft at the lowest until early Wednesday morning, by which POPs already start dropping off as the trough pushes east of us.

We'll see a lull in active weather on Thursday, with dry and mild conditions for SE Colorado. Highs will be in the 50s-60s again. Thursday Night and into the weekend, another, stronger system will begin moving in from the northwest. Latest model guidance still shows some inconsistency, though the trends suggest a broad upper trough carrying two separate portions of energy that will impact our region. POPs will pick up over the SW mountains again starting later Thursday Night, with more active weather lasting into early Saturday, though that could change depending on the evolution of the system. The system has also been trending more north, meaning that precipitation estimates have once again decreased for our CWA. While the San Juans will likely see some more accumulating snow, the rest of the area remains in flux in terms of QPF and related impacts.
Beyond this weekend, another broad trough appears to be on deck for early next week, though it is still far too early for details to become clear.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: A transient shortwave ridge will bring a temporary drying trend Wednesday, before the next upstream trough spreads inland Thursday. A fair amount of uncertainty remains regarding the evolution of this trough which will drive precip timing and amounts.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - There is a slight chance for excessive rainfall (level 1 of 4) across southern Utah on Tuesday, as a strong cold front sweeps through the region.

- Winter Weather Advisories are in effect for the Wasatch and western Uinta Mountains, and Southern Mountains where 4 to 10 inches of snow is expected through Tuesday night. A Winter Weather Advisory is also in effect for the Wasatch Back, where 1 to 4 inches of snow is expected.
- Another storm system will bring accumulating mountain snow Thursday into Friday, with snow levels potentially falling near or below 5000 feet by Friday.
- Freezing temperatures are increasing in probability for lower Washington County and the Virgin River corridor near Zion National Park Saturday and Sunday mornings

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A progressive shortwave trough currently translating through California and western NV will continue east overnight, before becoming negatively-tilted as it ejects across the forecast area Tuesday through Tuesday night. The result will be widespread valley rain and mountain snow across much of the forecast area through Tuesday, with snow levels likely falling to the benches of the Wasatch Front Tuesday evening.

As this wave approaches southwest Utah, increasing large scale forcing late tonight through Tuesday morning will result in widespread showers and occasional thunderstorms. The window for heaviest precipitation looks to be late morning through early afternoon as the low level baroclinic zone lifts through the area. Instances of heavy rain will be possible, and given moist antecedent conditions runoff should continue to be efficient. As such there is a Slight Risk of Excessive Rainfall (level 1 of 4) across much of southern Utah on Tuesday. Cooling temperatures through the afternoon will allow snow levels to fall from roughly 8500 feet Tuesday morning to around 7000 feet by late afternoon. The ejecting upper trough axis will allow drier mid-level air to quickly spread into the area mid to late afternoon which will limit snowfall duration, however elevations above 8000 feet still look to pick up 4-8", and the going Winter Weather Advisory looks reasonable.

Northern Utah will likely see two periods of organized precipitation as this system lifts through the region. The initial round will be tied to the lifting baroclinic zone, and will likely be accompanied by embedded convection as it quickly crosses the area midday. This will be followed by a period of more stratiform precipitation associated with the ejecting mid-level trough axis Tuesday afternoon/evening, with orographic precipitation lingering through the evening potentially into the overnight hours. Low level flow remains largely WNW to W through the evening which will likely limit orographic influence to some degree in the upper Cottonwoods. Additionally, hi-res guidance indicates the potential for lake enhanced showers late evening and overnight, which would largely impact Davis/Weber Counties, and perhaps northern Sale Lake.

In terms of snow levels, 700mb temperatures near -5C by late afternoon will fall near -8C through the evening, which will lower snow levels to the benches. It's not out of the question snow levels fall to the valley floors at times before precipitation winds down, particularly in heavier bands. Any accumulation will remain rate- driven and largely confined to grassy/elevated surfaces given warm surface temperatures, with the exception of the upper benches.

A transient shortwave ridge will bring a temporary drying trend Wednesday, before the next upstream trough spreads inland Thursday. A fair amount of uncertainty remains regarding the evolution of this trough which will drive precip timing and amounts.

2660.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Spencer Logan
bottom_line: Avalanche conditions are generally safe on Tuesday. Monitor afternoon warming. If you find wet snow surfaces, there is potential for small loose avalanches.
On shady slopes the current snowpack surface is weak and faceted. It will not take much new snow by Wednesday morning to make for easily triggered, small avalanches.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe and lack sufficient coverage for an avalanche. At high elevations, steer clear of isolated patches of firm, drifted snow below ridges or in steep gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has begun to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. 6-12 inches of new snow has fallen between Friday the 13th and Monday the 16th. Another 6-12 inches could stack up by the end of the week. If you're traveling in the mountains this week, watch out for wind slabs 1-2 feet thick above 7,000 feet and pay attention to terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: From 60-degree temperatures to over a foot of new snow, the weather sure has changed quickly over the past week. A cooler and wetter weather pattern has taken shape over our region since Friday the 13th. As of Monday (16th) afternoon, some mountain locations have picked up 6-12 inches of new snow along with southerly winds gusting 20-30 MPH.
Wind Slabs
• Wind slabs could become reactive this week with over a foot of new snow and gusty winds. Wind slabs will be most sensitive just below ridgelines.
• Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices.
• Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
• Strong winds and local terrain features can alter the prevailing wind direction. Pay attention to cross-loading and wind-loading on unsuspecting slopes.
Early Season Conditions
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.
Check Your Winter Gear

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
Continuing Education
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with the winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
Observations
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Keep an eye on increasing winds and snow transport throughout the day. If you find slightly stiffer, wind-blown drifts on a steeper slope at higher elevations, consider avoiding that terrain. There's a chance you could trigger a small avalanche in an isolated terrain feature.
